extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and patent examiners (U.S. practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the definition, timing, use, and strategic management of continuation, divisional, and continuation-in-part (CIP) patent applications in U.S. prosecution, including priority date effects, filing windows, portfolio strategy, and limitations such as double-patenting and patent term considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional applications (definition and protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: A divisional claims a distinct invention disclosed but not claimed in the parent, filed in response to a restriction requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains the cancelled claims (or equivalent); claims priority to the original application's filing date; examined separately; issues as a separate patent; protected by 35 USC 121 safe harbor (no double patenting). Use divisionals after a restriction requirement to pursue non-elected inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation applications (definition and requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuation application is a re-filing of an existing patent application that uses the same specification and claims priority to the parent's filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receives a new serial number; must have the same specification as the parent (no new matter); claims the same subject matter as the earlier parent but may be used to pursue new claims targeting different aspects. Continuations are useful to capture new claim scope or respond to competitor activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation-in-part (CIP) applications (definition and priority rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: A CIP includes new matter in addition to the parent's disclosure and mixes original and new disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New matter does not receive the parent's earlier filing date; original matter retains priority date. Each claim's priority date depends on which disclosure (original or new matter) supports that claim. CIPs are useful for incremental improvements added after the original filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic use: when to file each application type
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance mapping which continuing application type to use depending on prosecution circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisional: after a restriction requirement to pursue non-elected inventions. Continuation: to capture new claim scope, respond to competitor activities, or pursue broader/different claims. CIP: to incorporate post-filing improvements (new matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical timing requirements for continuing applications
rubrics_metrics.description: All continuation, divisional, and CIP applications must be filed while the earlier patent application is still pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a patent application is abandoned or a patent issues and the issue fee is paid, the window for filing most continuing applications closes. Best practice: file continuation before the issue fee is paid in the parent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority-date determination for claims (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim's effective priority date depends on the disclosure in the parent or application that supports the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For continuations and divisionals supported by the same specification, claims generally get the parent's filing date. For CIPs, only original matter gets the earlier date; new matter gets the CIP filing date. Each claim must be analyzed for whether it is supported by the earlier disclosure to determine its priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio management when drafting the parent
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the patent family tree at drafting to enable effective continuation/divisional practice and to cover commercial embodiments and design-arounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the specification supports divisional and continuation claims; cover competitor design-arounds; coordinate claim scope across family members; avoid over-breadth that invites invalidity challenges and avoid under-breadth that leaves commercial embodiments unprotected. Plan family strategy early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic continuation pendency (best practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain continuation pendency strategically to preserve prosecution flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: maintain at least one continuation in every family pending until the patent term expires to allow adapting claims to new infringers, capturing claim scope discovered during litigation, and responding to design-arounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions, limits, and double-patenting considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical and legal limits on continuing application practice and interactions with patent term and double-patenting rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO may try to limit continuation practice. Continuations cannot extend the patent term beyond the parent plus any RCE and applicable adjustments. Patent term adjustment (PTA) may differ between parent and continuation. If claims are not patentably distinct between applications, double-patenting issues arise and a terminal disclaimer may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution best practices specific to continuations/divisionals/CIPs
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational actions applicants should take when using continuing applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File continuations before the parent issue fee is paid; disclose all known prior art in continuations (duty of candor continues); consider request for continued examination (RCE) versus filing a continuation strategically; and carefully track the relationship between parent and continuations (family tree, claim dependencies, priority chains).
